title: The dog on a leash
hookLine: a dog tied to a post circles it endlessly: clinging to self (SN 22.99)

lines: ONE WAY AROUND, THEN THE OTHER.
cards: Outside a grocery store, a dog is tied to a post. Its person went in five minutes ago. The dog walks one way around the post, then the other, wrapping and unwrapping its leash, sitting, standing, circling again.
It's going somewhere and nowhere at once. Everyone who walks past smiles, because it's so clearly waiting for something it can't make happen faster.
The Buddha used that very picture, a dog tied to a stake, and he wasn't talking about dogs.

teach.b: SN 22.99 begins with a large claim. This round of wandering, the Buddha says, has no beginning that can be found. Beings roam on, blocked by not knowing, tied by craving.
A time may come when the great ocean dries up, when this great earth is burned up. Even so, the suffering of beings who wander like this doesn't end. Then the picture.

teach.h: A DOG TIED TO A STRONG POST
teach.b: Suppose a dog on a leash is tied to a strong post or pillar. It just runs and circles around that post.

In the same way, the untaught person regards the body as self, or self as having a body, or the body as inside the self, or the self as inside the body. The same with feeling, perception, formations, consciousness.
So they circle those five, and aren't freed from them.

teach.h: THE POST IS THE HEAPS, THE LEASH IS ME
teach.b: The post is the heaps. The leash is taking them as me. The dog isn't evil and isn't stupid.
It's just tied, and every lap it runs is real: moving, trying, hoping. The circle is set by the post. Those four ways are precise.
I am my body. I have a body. My body is in me.
I am in my body. The sutta says these are all ways of being tied. The good news is in the same picture.
A dog that isn't tied doesn't circle.
The text, here and in the next discourse, goes on: one who doesn't take the heaps as self isn't bound to the post.

how: Buddhist teachers often use the leash simile to explain identity view, the twenty ways of taking the five aggregates as self, which many traditions treat as the first fetter to be broken.

o: a post where travelers tie animals
a leash that ties a dog to a post

s: SN 22.99 says the ocean drying up would end beings' suffering
even when the ocean dries up and the earth burns, it says suffering doesn't end for those still wandering.
the sutta lists four ways of taking the body as self
body as self, self with a body, body in self, self in body.
the dog in the simile is called foolish
it isn't blamed; it's tied, and the circle is set by the post.

games.q: you're the dog, tied to a post, running in circles. by SN 22.99, what would let you stop?
o: not be tied: not take the heaps as self.
games.why: the circle comes from the leash. the texts say one who doesn't take the heaps as self isn't bound to the post.

practice: Notice one thought you keep circling, a worry about money, something someone said, and watch it come around again, the way the dog comes round the post. Then look for the post: what's it tied to?
Often it's a sense of me, my reputation, my plans; you don't have to cut the leash, just see it, and then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Gaddula. The Pali word for a leash or strap, the image in SN 22.99, where the untaught person circles the five heaps like a dog tied to a post, taking them as self. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali gaddula: a leash or strap. SN 22.99 is the Gaddulabaddha Sutta, the one bound by a leash.

carryVoice: Your line: round and round. Every lap is real, but the post sets the circle. See you tomorrow.
